column1: # npm-pre-scan evaluation corpus — REAL MALICIOUS PACKAGES (registry side)
# Purpose : real npm packages with published malicious-code advisories, scanned
#           through the live registry. Measures what Layer 0 can do against
# Source  : names cross-checked against ossf/malicious-packages (OSV MAL-*
#           records) and the 2017 npm typosquat campaign disclosure; every
#           `kind` below was verified live against registry.npmjs.org on
#           package"`, i.e. npm took the package down).
# npm's takedown process makes real malicious CODE unobtainable here:
#   kind=holder  npm replaced the package with a "security holding" stub
#                returns HTTP 200. Several of these RETAIN their original
#                version numbers with downloadable tarballs, but the content was
#                republished DEFANGED — verified 2026-07-30, the payload is
#                literally `console.log('this package is no longer dangerous')`.
#                So a content-layer PASS on these is truthful, not a detection
#                failure: the harness classifies it ARTIFACT_FN, never FN.
#                Only Layer 0's name-based checks are meaningfully exercised.
#   kind=name    fully unpublished (registry 404). Layer 0's name checks still
#                run (they need no network); registry checks are skipped.
# Real malicious PAYLOADS for Layers 1-3 come from the DataDog corpus instead —
# `vectors` records the attack class as documented in the disclosure (ground
# truth), NOT a prediction that our detector fires. Whether A1 actually catches
# `d3.js` is exactly what the experiment measures.
# --- 2017 typosquat campaign (Aug 2017, ~40 packages by one actor) -----------
# Stole environment variables via postinstall. All taken down; parents in
# --- Reclaimed names: benign TODAY, so a flag here is a genuine FALSE POSITIVE
# These three were part of the campaign but the names were later taken over by
# legitimate projects, so `label=benign` reflects what the registry serves now.
